review_scope: Full 30-line command-line concept plus complete permission and multi-branch note read. Supported-secret and preexisting-alert exceptions retained. Linked resolution, bypass, sensitive-data and Git configuration pages remain unresolved; no actual runtime receipt.

claims.statement: Command-line blocking is described for supported secrets and repositories secured by push protection, not arbitrary sensitive content or all repositories.
The documented blocked-push response offers removing the secret from the branch; actual history cleanup and credential invalidation are distinct actions.
The blocked-push response offers a URL for available bypass or privilege-request options; the existence of an option is not approval to bypass.
The command line displays up to five detected secrets at a time; displayed count is not the complete detection denominator.
The article says a secret already detected with an existing repository alert is not blocked again; a permitted push therefore cannot prove no supported secrets are present.
A real-secret fix-later bypass should be remediated promptly, rather than treated as completed merely because the push succeeded.
The article requires revocation of exposed real secrets to prevent unauthorized access; removing repository bytes alone does not revoke access.
The article presents rotation before revocation as a consideration and history removal as an example, not automatic authority for credential or destructive history changes.
The command-line article's permission fragment identifies users with write access; actual effective access and bypass eligibility remain separate.
Multi-branch Git push configuration may include unintended refs that trigger a block; verification must account for all pushed refs, not only the current branch.
The timeout note describes post-push secret scanning when push-time scanning times out; retrospective scanning is not proof that pre-push prevention succeeded.
